title: In a literature-based mass and flux budget, normal transmitter release changes the MRS glutamate signal by amounts about 10 to 160 times smaller than event-related fMRS studies report
abstract:
Normal release of the transmitter glutamate in the human brain is far too small to explain the fast changes of 11-22% in the glutamate signal that event-related functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) studies report. This matters because event-related fMRS (MRS repeated during a task, with spectra sorted by short trial events) is used as the main non-invasive, transmitter-specific measure of fast brain activity.

We made a mass and flux budget from published values: synapse density, vesicles per synapse, molecules per vesicle, the 13C-MRS glutamate-glutamine cycle rate, firing rates, release probability, and energy and metabolic fluxes. We assumed the most favourable mechanism: released transmitter moves from fully MRS-invisible vesicles to fully visible pools. Over 200,000 Monte Carlo draws, normal activity changes the signal by 0.10% of voxel glutamate within 3 s (95% range 0.018-0.51%). If release accumulates over a block or run of 36-300 s, the 97.5th percentile is 4.7-5.5%. A seizure-like hard ceiling (every synapse at maximal release, plus the largest metabolic fluxes) gives 1.9% within 3 s.

All 7 reported event-related glutamate or Glx (glutamate plus glutamine) values (11.5-21.5%; 4 studies and a pooled mean) are larger than the physiological estimate in at least 99.9% of draws. At the longest window each design allows, the median factor is 10-34; it is 165 for the one design with interleaved trial types, which also exceeds the hard ceiling by a factor of 6. Designs against separate rest blocks or runs reach the hard ceiling at long windows, but mainly through metabolism, not release. A significant 12.7% GABA decrease exceeds the physiological estimate in 99.6% of draws; a 6.8% decrease is not excluded. Block-design glutamate rises (1.8-5.3%) fit a metabolic origin.

The empirical standard error of the interleaved design is 6.7 times the value that spectral fitting precision predicts. At the physiological effect, power is 5%, about half of significant results have the wrong sign, and significant results overstate the effect 100-270 times. This work extends a published one-vesicle estimate with time-resolved release capacity, accumulation, uncertainty and design statistics. Main limit: the budget does not exclude a fast visibility change that release does not cause.

Filled symbols: reported event-related changes at the within-trial window; open symbols: the same changes at the contrast window, where release can accumulate over a block or run. Diamonds: block designs. Absolute values are shown. C: reported change divided by each bound (median; line to the 2.5th percentile), with summed increase and decrease bounds for contrasts between two active conditions.

A: smallest significant group effect (two-sided p = 0.05, 12 subjects, 8 mL voxel) against acquisitions per condition per subject, with precision from published Cramer-Rao bounds and with an extra variance term calibrated on the reported statistics of Lally et al. 2014 (black point: that design and its reported 11.5% effect). B: glutamate signals and errors: physiological release-linked change and hard ceiling in 3 s, BOLD line-shape bias with and without correction (Wilson et al. 2026), group standard error, and reported values.
